topics.title: One number as the state
topics.about: The whole past is summed up by a single number: the total so far, or the number that is left.

topics.title: Coins and knapsacks
topics.about: Items and a budget. Ordered or unordered, once or many times, best value or yes and no: the loops decide.

topics.title: Grids
topics.about: A cell is reached from the cells that lead into it.

topics.title: A position and a little more
topics.about: Going left to right, with one small extra fact carried along.

topics.title: Two sequences
topics.about: A prefix of one against a prefix of the other.

topics.title: Intervals and shapes
topics.about: The state is a stretch, or a rectangle, and the choice is how to split it.

topics.title: Sort first, then a table
topics.about: Subsequences, schedules and heights: the right order of evaluation is half the solution.

topics.title: Subsets, profiles and digits
topics.about: States that are sets, column profiles, or prefixes of a number.

problems.title: Dice Combinations
problems.name: Count by the last move
problems.statement: Split the ways of reaching a total by their last step. Each group is a smaller instance of the same question, so one array indexed by the total is enough.
problems.remark: The empty total counts as one way. That single base value is what makes the sums come out right.

problems.title: Minimizing Coins
problems.name: Unreachable is a value too
problems.statement: The same table as for counting, with a minimum in place of a sum. Totals that cannot be made need their own value (infinity), and it must never be extended by accident.
problems.remark: Largest-coin-first is wrong for general coin systems; the table tries every last coin.

problems.title: Removing Digits
problems.name: The number itself is the state
problems.statement: The state does not have to be an index into the input: here it is the current number, and the moves are read off its digits.
problems.remark: Subtracting the largest digit happens to be optimal here, but the table needs no such insight and costs almost nothing.

problems.title: Coin Combinations I
problems.name: Ordered sums: total outside, coins inside
problems.statement: When different orders count as different ways, a way is determined by its last coin and what came before: for each total, add over all coins.
problems.remark: It is the dice problem with arbitrary faces.

problems.title: Coin Combinations II
problems.name: Unordered sums: coins outside, total inside
problems.statement: When order does not matter, fix an order in which coins may be used. Processing one coin at a time over all totals counts every multiset exactly once.
problems.remark: Swapping the two loops is the entire difference between the two coin-counting problems.

problems.title: Book Shop
problems.name: One row, filled downwards
problems.statement: Each item once, best value per budget: one array over the budget, updated from high budget to low so that an item cannot be taken twice.
problems.remark: A full table over items and budgets would be a hundred million cells; the single row is what fits in memory and in time.

problems.title: Money Sums
problems.name: A table of yes and no
problems.statement: Which totals can be made is the same knapsack with true and false as the values.
problems.remark: The table is as long as the largest possible total, not as the number of subsets.

problems.title: Two Sets II
problems.name: Count subsets, then undo the double counting
problems.statement: Splitting into two equal halves is choosing a subset with half the total. Every split is found twice, once from each side.
problems.remark: Halving modulo a prime needs an inverse; or avoid it by deciding in advance which side the largest number is on.

problems.title: Grid Paths I
problems.name: A cell from its two predecessors
problems.statement: The number of routes into a cell is the sum over the cells that can step into it; a blocked cell has none.
problems.remark: Check the start cell too: if it is blocked the answer is zero.

problems.title: Minimal Grid Path
problems.name: Advance a frontier of the best
problems.statement: When the value being optimised is a string, do not store strings. Move diagonal by diagonal, keeping only the cells that can still lie on a best path.
problems.remark: All candidates on a diagonal have spelled the same string so far, which is why the cells alone are enough.

problems.title: Array Description
problems.name: Position and the last value
problems.statement: When the rule links neighbours, the state is the position together with the value placed there.
problems.remark: A known value simply has one allowed state at its position.

problems.title: Counting Towers
problems.name: The state is the shape of the top
problems.statement: Build upwards and remember only what the top edge looks like: one wide block or two separate ones. Count the ways each shape leads to each shape.
problems.remark: With many queries, fill the table once up to the largest height.

problems.title: Edit Distance
problems.name: Prefix against prefix
problems.statement: The answer for two prefixes comes from the three ways of dealing with their last characters: match or replace, delete, insert.
problems.remark: The borders are not zero: turning a prefix into nothing costs its length.

problems.title: Longest Common Subsequence
problems.name: Walk the table back
problems.statement: The table of lengths already contains an answer. Start at the final cell and repeatedly step to a cell that explains its value.
problems.remark: To walk back, the whole table must be kept.

problems.title: Removal Game
problems.name: The mover's lead on an interval
problems.statement: For a game on a shrinking interval, store the best possible difference (mover minus opponent). Taking an end gives that number minus the opponent's best lead on what remains.
problems.remark: The first player's score is half of the total plus the lead.

problems.title: Rectangle Cutting
problems.name: Try every first cut
problems.statement: The state is the pair of side lengths; the first cut splits it into two smaller rectangles that are solved independently.
problems.remark: Cutting off the largest square each time is not optimal.

problems.title: Increasing Subsequence
problems.name: The smallest ending for each length
problems.statement: Keep, for every length, the smallest value an increasing subsequence of that length can end with. The list is sorted, and each new element changes one entry, found by binary search.
problems.remark: For strictly increasing, replace the first entry that is not smaller than the new element.

problems.title: Increasing Subsequence II
problems.name: Sum over smaller values
problems.statement: The number of increasing subsequences ending at an element is one plus the sum of the counts at earlier, smaller elements: a prefix sum over values, kept in a Fenwick tree.
problems.remark: Values up to a billion are first replaced by their ranks.

problems.title: Projects
problems.name: Sort by end, then take or skip
problems.statement: Sorted by ending day, each project is either skipped or taken together with the best result among projects that end before it starts, found by binary search.
problems.remark: Two projects that share a day clash.

problems.title: Mountain Range
problems.name: Evaluate in order of height
problems.statement: The states are the mountains, but a mountain depends on lower ones, wherever they stand. Process by increasing height; what a mountain can reach is the stretch between its nearest neighbours that are at least as tall.
problems.remark: The best value over a stretch needs a range-maximum structure.

problems.title: Elevator Rides
problems.name: A pair as the value
problems.statement: For each set of people already taken up, store the pair (rides used, weight in the last ride), smallest first. Adding a person either fits in the last ride or starts a new one.
problems.remark: A million sets times twenty people is the whole computation.

problems.title: Counting Tilings
problems.name: A profile of what sticks out
problems.statement: Go through the grid column by column. The only memory needed is which cells of the next column are already covered by tiles sticking out of this one: a mask.
problems.remark: The mask runs along the short side.

problems.title: Counting Numbers
problems.name: Up to b, minus up to a - 1
problems.statement: A count over a range is a difference of two counts from zero. Each of those is built digit by digit, remembering the previous digit, whether the limit still binds, and whether the number has started.
problems.remark: Leading zeros are not digits of the number.
